questions.question: Define a field in a DBMS.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • A field is the smallest meaningful unit of data in a database.
  • • It stores one specific attribute of a record. e.g., Name, Age, Roll Number in a student record.
  • ((1 mark) for definition + (1 mark) for example)
  • Domain
  • • The set of all permitted atomic values for an attribute.
  • • Defines the data type and valid range for a column.
  • • Examples: Domain of Age = positive integers 1–120; Domain of Department = {Science, Arts
  • Commerce}.
questions.final_answer: Commerce}
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Explain one-to-one relationship with an example.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Each record in Table A is linked to exactly one record in Table B, and vice versa.
  • • Example: One person has one passport; one student has one ID card.
  • • Implemented using a Foreign Key with a UNIQUE constraint.
  • ((1 mark) for definition + (1 mark) for example)
  • Attribute
  • • A named column in a relation, associated with a specific domain.
  • • Describes one property of the entity being stored.
  • • Example: STUDENT table has attributes StudentID, Name, Age, Department. Degree = number of
  • attributes.
questions.final_answer: attributes

questions.question: Differentiate between a single line and a dashed line in an ER diagram.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Single line (solid line): Represents partial participation — not all entity instances must participate in the
  • relationship.
  • • Double line (two parallel lines): Represents total participation — every entity instance must participate.
  • • Dashed ellipse: Represents a derived attribute (e.g., Age derived from Date of Birth).
  • • Dashed underline: Represents the discriminator (partial key) of a weak entity.
  • • Note: The question contrasts 'single line' with 'dashed line' — single line = partial participation; dashed
  • elements = derived attribute or discriminator.
  • ((1 mark) for single line = partial participation + (1 mark) for dashed line/element with correct meaning)
  • Tuple
  • • A single row in a relation representing one real-world entity instance.
  • • Contains exactly one value per attribute.
  • • Example: (101, 'Arjun Menon', 20, 'Science') is one tuple in STUDENT. Cardinality = number of tuples.
questions.final_answer: • Example: (101, 'Arjun Menon', 20, 'Science') is one tuple in STUDENT. Cardinality = number of tuples

questions.question: Name the components of a MySQL table.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Columns (Fields) — store individual attributes
  • • Rows (Records / Tuples) — one complete entry
  • • Primary Key — uniquely identifies each row
  • • Data Types — define kind of data per column (INT, VARCHAR, DATE, etc.)
  • • Constraints — rules like NOT NULL, UNIQUE, DEFAULT, FOREIGN KEY
  • (Any 4 components — ½ mark each)
  • Relation
  • • A complete two-dimensional table with a schema (structure) and an instance (current data).
  • • Properties: all cell values are atomic; column names are unique; no duplicate rows; row/column order
  • does not matter.
  • • Example: STUDENT (StudentID, Name, Age, Department) — schema; all current student rows —
  • instance.
questions.final_answer: instance

questions.question: Explain how DBMS reduces data redundancy.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Data redundancy = same data stored in multiple places, causing waste and inconsistency.
  • • DBMS reduces redundancy through
  • • Centralised storage: All data stored once; all applications access the same source.
  • • Normalisation: Tables are organised so each fact is stored exactly once.
  • • Foreign Keys: Tables reference each other instead of repeating data (e.g., DeptID in EMPLOYEE table
  • instead of full department details).
  • • Data Dictionary: DBMS tracks all stored data, preventing accidental duplication.
  • • Example: Student phone number stored once in STUDENT table; other tables refer by student ID only.
  • ((1 mark) for defining redundancy + (1 mark) each for 4 methods)
questions.final_answer: ( for defining redundancy + each for 4 methods)
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

questions.question: Differentiate between data and information with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Data: Raw, unprocessed facts with no meaning on their own.
  • • Information: Processed, organised data that is meaningful and useful for decision-making.
  • • Differences
  • • Data is input; information is output of processing.
  • • Data has no context; information has meaning and purpose.
  • • Data alone is not useful; information supports decisions.
  • • Examples
  • • Data: 85, 70, 90 → Information: Marks of three students in Chemistry.
  • • Data: 9846000000 → Information: Mobile number of the lab assistant.
  • • Data: Monday, 38, 12 → Information: On Monday, 38 attended class; 12 were late.
  • ((2 marks) for definitions + (3 marks) for differences and examples)
questions.final_answer: ( for definitions + for differences and examples)

questions.question: Describe how referential integrity ensures the connection between two related / tables.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Referential integrity ensures that a Foreign Key (FK) value in a child table always matches a valid
  • Primary Key (PK) value in the parent table, or is NULL.
  • • Rules enforced
  • • Insertion rule: A record cannot be added to the child table with a FK value that does not exist in the
  • parent table.
  • • Deletion rule: A parent record cannot be deleted if child records still reference it.
  • • Update rule: A PK value in the parent table cannot be changed if child records still refer to it (unless
  • CASCADE is set).
  • • Example: In a library DB, LOAN.MemberID (FK) references MEMBER.MemberID (PK). A loan
  • cannot be added for a non-existent member.
  • ((2 marks) for definition + (3 marks) for rules/example)
questions.final_answer: ( for definition + for rules/example)

questions.question: Describe a scenario where partial dependency and transitive dependency / occurs.
questions.solution_html:
• Answer
  • • Table: ENROLMENT (StudentID, CourseID, StudentName, CourseName, Marks, DeptID, DeptName)
  • • Primary Key: {StudentID, CourseID}
  • Partial Dependency
  • • StudentName depends only on StudentID (part of PK) — not on the full composite key.
  • • CourseName depends only on CourseID (part of PK) — not on the full composite key.
  • • Non-key attribute depends on only part of the composite primary key.
  • Transitive Dependency
  • • DeptName depends on DeptID, and DeptID depends on StudentID.
  • • DeptName is not directly dependent on the primary key — it goes through a non-key attribute (DeptID).
  • • Chain: {StudentID, CourseID} → DeptID → DeptName
  • • Fix: Decompose into STUDENT, COURSE, ENROLMENT (StudentID, CourseID, Marks)
  • DEPARTMENT tables.
  • ((2.5 marks) for partial dependency with example + (2.5 marks) for transitive dependency with example)
questions.final_answer: ( for partial dependency with example + for transitive dependency with example)

  • are HR, IT, Finance

questions.question: Explain the UPDATE statement in MySQL. Demonstrate how to update a single / column, multiple columns, and update based on a condition with examples.
questions.solution_html:
• columns, and update based on a condition with examples. ((5 marks))
  • Answer
  • • UPDATE modifies existing records in a table.
  • • Syntax: UPDATE table_name SET column = value WHERE condition;
  • • Without WHERE, all rows are updated — usually unintended.

questions.question: Using the table EMPLOYEE(EmpID, Name, Department, Salary), write SQL / queries to demonstrate: WHERE clause to filter employees with Salary > 30000, (b) ORDER BY to sort employees by Name, (c) GROUP BY to count employees per department, (d) HAVING to show departments with more than 2 employees, (e) LIKE to find employees whose name starts with 'A', (f) BETWEEN to find employees with salary between 20000 and 50000.Explain the purpose of each clause.
questions.solution_html:
• Using EMPLOYEE(EmpID, Name, Department, Salary), write SQL queries for: (a) WHERE, (b) ORDER
  • BY, (c) GROUP BY, (d) HAVING, (e) LIKE, (f) BETWEEN. Explain the purpose of each clause. (15
  • marks)
  • Answer
  • • Table: EMPLOYEE (EmpID, Name, Department, Salary)
  • (a) WHERE
  • • Purpose: Filters rows based on a condition; only matching rows are returned.
  • SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Salary > 30000;
  • • Returns all employees earning more than 30,000.
  • (b) ORDER BY
  • • Purpose: Sorts the result set. Default is ASC (ascending); use DESC for descending.
  • SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE ORDER BY Name ASC;
  • • Returns all employees sorted alphabetically by name.
  • (c) GROUP BY
  • • Purpose: Groups rows with the same column value. Used with aggregate functions like COUNT, SUM
  • AVG.
  • SELECT Department, COUNT(*) AS EmpCount FROM EMPLOYEE GROUP BY Department;
  • • Returns count of employees in each department.
  • (d) HAVING
  • • Purpose: Filters groups formed by GROUP BY. Like WHERE but applied after grouping.
  • SELECT Department, COUNT(*) AS EmpCount FROM EMPLOYEE
  • GROUP BY Department HAVING COUNT(*) > 2;
  • • Returns only departments with more than 2 employees.
  • (e) LIKE
  • • Purpose: Pattern matching on text columns. % = any number of characters; _ = exactly one character.
  • SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';
  • • Returns all employees whose name starts with 'A' (e.g., Arjun, Amal, Athira).
  • (f) BETWEEN
  • • Purpose: Selects rows where a value falls within an inclusive range.
  • SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Salary BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000;
  • • Returns employees with salary from 20,000 to 50,000 (both values included).
  • ((2.5 marks) per clause: (1 mark) purpose + (1 mark) correct query + (0.5 mark) output explanation)
  • Sumaja Sasidharan
  • Asst.Professor
  • Sree Sankara Vidyapeetom College
  • Valayanchirangara
questions.final_answer: Option WHERE, (b) ORDER
questions.source_exam: MGU-UGP (HONOURS) 2024 Admission Regular Exam Sem 4, March 2026

  • • Purpose: Pattern matching on text columns. % = any number of characters; _ = exactly one character.
  • SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Name LIKE 'A%';
  • • Returns all employees whose name starts with 'A' (e.g., Arjun, Amal, Athira).
  • (f) BETWEEN
  • • Purpose: Selects rows where a value falls within an inclusive range.
  • SELECT * FROM EMPLOYEE WHERE Salary BETWEEN 20000 AND 50000;
  • • Returns employees with salary from 20,000 to 50,000 (both values included).
  • ((2.5 marks) per clause: (1 mark) purpose + (1 mark) correct query + (0.5 mark) output explanation)
